How the win rate is actually produced

graded by how strongly the record supports each one

He is a competent trader with a real process. The mechanics below are ordered by how much of the headline number each one explains — and two of them are weaker than they look from the outside.

strongly supported

Discretionary early exit - he can always choose to book, and he only chooses when green

This is the structural fact that produces the win rate. He does not usually leave a resting take-profit; he closes manually when he sees a rejection, a wick, a stall, or simply wants the slot. Because the decision to close is his and the decision to lose is the stop's, discretionary exits are one-directional: they convert unrealised green into a recorded win and never into a recorded loss. Losses can only arrive the one way he cannot veto - through a stop. The cost is that he leaves the tail of every winner on the table, which is exactly why his average R is small.

Exit types across 217 positions: manual_close 62, take_profit 45, stop_loss 35, breakeven 11, unknown 43. Of the 62 manual closes, 61 are wins, 1 is breakeven, 0 are losses. All 35 losses closed at a stop. Only 45 of 120 wins (38%) reached a target he had published; at least 26 wins were manual closes booked short of the stated TP. There are more manual closes than take-profits.
supported

Small targets held for a short time

He trades for a fraction of the stop distance and gets out fast. A 0.5R target on a scalp needs only a small favourable move, so a high proportion of entries reach it before the stop, and the median position is closed inside a day. He is explicit that this is a deliberate trade of R for hit rate, and that the arithmetic only works because of frequency. His own stated 0.5-0.8R average is lower than what the record shows on the wins where he published an R, so the honest version is 'roughly 1R targets on the wins he reports, with a genuine 0.5R scalp book underneath'.

31 messages state a 0.5-0.8R figure. Of 120 wins, only 27 carry a stated R: median 1.00R, mean 1.05R; 11 of 27 are <=0.8R, 8 are exactly 0.5R, 2 are >=2R. Median hold 17.2 hours, mean 33.9, max 453. That stated-R sample is self-selected - he reports R when it flatters.
supported

A long-biased book in a market that mostly went up

Roughly three of every four positions are longs, and he says so plainly. Across the sample BTC fell from the high 70s to the high 50s and then recovered past its starting point, and his win rate rises monotonically through that recovery. A directional book with a small target does well when the direction is right; the same book is what produced his worst stretch, when he shorted against his own bullish view and took five stops in two days. The bias is a genuine edge in this regime and an unhedged exposure in another.

152 longs vs 47 shorts among the 200 taken positions (3.2:1); 106 long vs 33 short among 139 signal posts. Longs won 78% of resolved outcomes excluding breakevens, shorts 74%. Monthly win rate excluding breakevens: May 73%, June 76%, July 82%, August 83%.
supported

Every trade ships with a stop and a size before it is entered

Whatever happens afterwards, the setup is fully specified at the moment of entry: a price, a stop, usually a target, often a DCA level, and always a size instruction. He teaches position sizing off a risk calculator rather than off leverage, and he publishes a stop on nine out of ten trades. This is ordinary, unglamorous, and the most replicable thing in the entire record - and it is why the losses, when they come, are bounded and single.

Of the 200 positions he took: 180 (90%) had a published stop, 118 (59%) a published target, 57 (29%) a published DCA level. 139 signal-format posts follow the same fixed template. Only 15 widen/remove/hard-to-manual stop events across 217 positions (7%).
supported

Trade selection: he stops when he is ahead and caps concurrent risk

He refuses setups he rates highly when too many positions are already open, closes trades purely to reduce clutter, and stops posting entirely once a weekly or monthly target is met. Each of these is defensible risk behaviour and each also acts as a filter on which trades ever reach the scoreboard. The clutter closures in particular land in the manual-close bucket, which contains no losses.

16 of the 217 catalogued setups were posted but never taken by him. He declines on position-count grounds in at least msgs 24, 48, 187, 706, and coasts after hitting a target in msgs 701, 843, 875, 878.
strongly supported

The scoreboard is generous - part of the headline number is accounting, not trading

The reconstructed record is good; the published record is better. His summaries dropped the breakeven category he used to keep, understate the loss count in both months he reported, resolve ambiguous outcomes at his discretion, and exclude entire classes of trade declared unofficial before the fact. This does not make the trading fake - a 77% reconstructed win rate is a real result - but a reader comparing himself to 85-90% is comparing himself to a number that was never audited.

Claimed May 85% (51W/9L/60) vs reconstructed 73% (36W/13L/1BE). Claimed July 89% (40W/5SL/45) vs reconstructed 82% (31W/7L/3BE); claimed 93% on BTC vs 87% reconstructed. Whole sample: 120W/35L/10BE = 77% excluding breakevens. No June summary was ever posted.
weak

A reserved DCA tranche as a rescue tool

AUDIT-DOWNGRADED. The draft called the reserved tranche 'the mechanism that turns a losing entry into a winner'. It does rescue individual trades, visibly and sometimes dramatically, but it is used on a minority of positions and the positions that use it perform WORSE than those that do not. It cannot be the engine of the win rate. The reason is not mysterious: a DCA fills precisely when the original entry was wrong, so the cohort is pre-selected for bad entries.

53 of 139 signal posts (38%) publish a DCA level; 57 of 200 taken positions plan one; only 30 (14%) ever fill one. DCA-filled positions: 19W / 9L = 68%. Positions with no DCA fill: 101W / 26L / 10BE = 80% excluding breakevens.
weak

Soft and moveable stops

AUDIT-DOWNGRADED. Vividly real as behaviour and genuinely decisive on the handful of occasions it fires - removing a published BTC stop outright, holding past a stop he had told followers about, running a stopless ETH short - but far too rare to explain the headline win rate. Nine signals in ten carry a plain numeric stop, and all 35 of his losses closed at one. The right reading is that this is his biggest single risk to a follower, not his biggest single edge.

Only 14 of 139 signal posts (10%) publish a candle-close soft SL; 10 publish the soft+hard pair. Across 217 positions there are 45 stop moves, of which 15 (7% of positions) are a widen, extend, remove or hard-to-manual switch. 22 positions carry a to-entry stop move against ~44 messages instructing it.

His scoreboard against the record

His published scoreboard and the reconstructed record do not agree, and the gap is not explained by trade management. Reconstructing every position he posted gives 217 catalogued setups, 200 actually taken, 165 with a knowable outcome: 120 wins, 35 losses, 10 breakevens - 77% excluding breakevens, 73% including them. His own monthly summaries claim 85% (May) and 89% (July). The published figures run 8-13 points hot, and understate the loss count in both months he reported. The direction of travel in the record is real and favourable - monthly win rate rises 73% (May), 76% (June), 82% (July), 83% (August) - so this is a competent trader with a genuinely good hit rate whose accounting flatters an already-good number rather than inventing one. Three structural facts do most of the work: the breakeven bucket disappeared from his summaries once he had an audience, ambiguous outcomes are resolved at his discretion, and whole categories of trade are declared 'unofficial' before the fact.

What he actually watches

count = messages that mention it

The toolkit is thin on purpose. No RSI, no fibonacci, no order flow, no open interest — those words never appear in four months of messages. Levels, candle closes, a 200 EMA and the calendar do nearly all the work.

Candle-close stops and confirmation (almost always the 4h close)

35×

He gives a 'soft SL' (a 4h close beyond the level) plus a wider 'hard SL' underneath it so a wick cannot take him out, and refuses to accept a stop until the candle actually closes. The same rule is used to stay in a losing trade ('mentioned will wait for 4h close hence I didn't take SL') and to decide whether a level is reclaimed. AUDIT CORRECTION: this is his most-cited piece of chart logic in commentary (35 messages), but it is a minority structure in his published signals - only 14 of 139 signal posts (10%) carry a candle-close stop and only 10 carry the soft+hard pair. Nine signals in ten use a plain numeric stop. It matters most when a trade is going against him, as the reason not to accept a stop.

technical

200 EMA (mostly 4h, also 15m/daily) as the line in the sand

14×

He converts the 200 EMA into a hard price level and builds the whole trade around it ('we shouldn't lose the 200 ema on 4h that is 77.7k'). A reclaim is a long trigger and a reason to expect repeat bounces; sitting on it is a reason to expect a bounce back to entry rather than take a stop. He also cites EMA 20 and EMA 50 as intraday bounce/rejection points.

technical

New daily low sweep then bounce ('dead cat bounce on LTF')

5×

When BTC is dumping he waits for a new daily low rather than buying into weakness, then longs the bounce and takes a fast 0.5-1R. The same idea appears as 'lows are swept you can add around 25% margin'. Two of his best-timed BTC longs (59.2k on 24 Jun, 58.2k on 25 Jun) came from this. NOTE ON WORDING: he uses 'swept' only once in 1,005 messages (msg 382); the other instances are the same idea in his own plain language ('they'll make a new daily low then bounce it'). The frequency of 5 is a count of the concept, not the word.

technical

Prior daily high / daily low as the anchor for both stops and targets

5×

On shorts the daily high is the stop; on longs the daily low is the stop. He explicitly tells followers to read the level off their own venue because of price differences. The same extreme in the other direction is the natural target ('can visit previous daily high'). AUDIT CORRECTION: the item was previously filed as stop placement only, with a target quote (msg 33) as its lead evidence and first_seen anchor; it now covers both uses explicitly.

technical

Round-number k-levels on BTC as an entry/TP grid

47×

He publishes an entry at CMP, a DCA 500-1500 lower and a TP at the next round number, then closes there manually. He also narrates price paths purely as level sequences ('65.3-65.6k over the weekend, then 62-63k, then 66-67k') and grades himself on whether the sequence played out. He explicitly boasts about not using charts. Quantitative support for the no-charts claim: of 320 attached images only 23 (7%) are charts, against 247 PnL share cards.

technical

Weekend / Sunday-Monday pump seasonality

14×

He holds longs into weekends specifically for this ('I'm this close to completely closing it but I think we are in for a Sunday pump'), sizes down for weekend risk ('WEEKEND SIZE, recommended half risk'), and structures shorts to survive the weekend pump instead of avoiding it. Alt calls on Friday are justified by 'coins that look ready for a weekend PUMP'.

time-based

Scheduled macro events (CPI, FOMC, monthly close)

8×

He positions before the event when he has a directional view ('opening it right before FOMC... either half risk or skip but I'm in'), moves SL to BE ahead of events he is unsure about, and warns of volatility on monthly close. He treats the post-event impulse as the payoff ('1400$ move caught, that's how we trade CPI').

fundamental

Geopolitical / headline catalysts (ceasefire, deals, Trump, Saylor)

12×

He pre-announces expected news ('a deal is coming this Sunday, free money, keep longing'), attributes moves to specific headlines after the fact, and will hold a losing position because a catalyst is due tomorrow. He also cuts shorting entirely around an event he thinks is bullish.

fundamental

BTC as the driver of every altcoin position

14×

Alt entries are justified with 'if BTC stabilizes/bounces this pumps', and alt losses are attributed to BTC ('started great but BTC ruining it'). He sizes alts down when BTC looks weak and closes alts pre-emptively when he expects BTC to reverse.

intermarket

Relative strength: alts that hold up during a BTC dump

6×

'Holding well against this dump' is his stated reason to long JUP; the same logic is applied to BOME, XPL, WLD and HYPE. The implied trade is that when BTC bounces, the strong coin gives the outsized move.

technical

Buy supports, do not chase pumps

8×

When he does take an already-pumped coin he explicitly halves size and says so ('already too pumped and I usually long supports only'). His best-described setup is 'daily support + EMA's were aligned, was breaking out'. Conversely a market that has run hard triggers half risk on new longs.

technical

Rejection / wick at a level as the manual exit trigger

9×

'I close around 62 (or until I see a rejection)'; 'if you see rejection after 64k immediately book it because that's resistance too'. He also tells followers to grab wicks when he is asleep ('If you see wicks try to TP'). This converts the exit into a discretionary, level-based decision.

technical

'Front run' — the belief that his own published levels get pre-empted

4×

He repeatedly cancels or skips limits that were 'front ran', enters CMP instead ('I don't want to take my chances front ran'), and posts the trade after he is filled. It is his stated reason for the CMP-first entry style.

orderflow

Fading the crowd's positioning in chat

6×

When 'everyone else is shorting' he stays long and posts his green position as proof; when many members want to short a coin he tells them to long it instead. He also declares 'don't force short' and 'don't short blindly' at the point where the crowd is bearish.

sentiment

LTF vs HTF split: wait on lower timeframe, position on higher

6×

'LTF looks bearish so waiting for entry' — he delays a planned setup rather than entering immediately, and tells followers not to place limits until he confirms. He separately offers 5m entries as unofficial ideas that will not be counted in his record.

technical

A separate gold/oil book, deliberately excluded from the crypto tally

8×

AUDIT CORRECTION - this item was previously framed as an intermarket signal. Only one message in 1,005 makes the gold->BTC inference, and he hedges it as 'just a thought' (msg 424). He never traded crypto off it. What the evidence actually shows is a separate forex book, posted on request from chat, with its own summary: 'I won't count gold trades in crypto summary but will make separate summary for these trades' (msg 405). This matters for the record-keeping picture more than for the method.

instrument

The rules he trades by

Risk

  • Risks 1-2% on alts, 3-5% on BTC. EXPLICIT AND OFTEN REPEATED - this is his headline teaching, stated identically in May, July and again on 31 Jul. Earliest version was '2% on normal trades and 1% on risky ones'. AUDIT CORRECTION: the playbook's 'BEHAVIOURAL CONTRADICTION' is DROPPED - both legs collapse on inspection. The 10-20% risk is a disclosed, ring-fenced $89.36 novelty account he announced as a 'for fun' 2x challenge and explicitly told members not to copy (msg 221). The +30.92%-in-four-days curve captioned 'This is where I risk only 3-5% per trade' is arithmetically consistent with 3-5% risk, because the message immediately before it posts the exchange's own stats panel for that same window showing 11 closed orders and 11 winners. Nothing in 1,005 messages shows him exceeding his stated risk on his main book. The honest finding is that he discloses the carve-out.
  • Size every trade with a position-size calculator; leverage is irrelevant. EXPLICIT. He posted a step-by-step tutorial (wallet, risk %, entry, SL -> coin quantity), told members to set orders 'By Amount' on the exchange, and argued that once the coin quantity is right the leverage number does not matter. The observed leverage on his own share cards is nevertheless extreme (150x most common, 250x, 300x, 500x seen), which is consistent with the claim only if margin is tiny.
  • 'Half risk' / 'weekend size' tag on anything he judges risky. EXPLICIT AND HEAVILY USED - 54 messages on the broad pattern (half risk / half margin / weekend size / go low / small margin / risk half). He grades each call and attaches a size instruction: half risk for risky setups, shitcoins, pumped markets, weekends, pre-FOMC, wide or manual stops, and anything against his own directional bias. This is his main risk lever, applied per-trade rather than through stop distance. WORTH NAMING: the label is also used retrospectively, after a loss, to assign responsibility for the outcome to the follower's sizing - 'mentioned it was risky so hopefully risk was managed' (msg 639), 'If anyone used half risk as I mentioned I promise we will use full risk and quickly recover' (msg 997).
  • Soft SL (4h close) plus a wider hard SL to survive liquidation wicks. EXPLICIT but a minority structure. On some trades he gives two stops: a discretionary one on a 4h close and a hard order further away, whose stated purpose is anti-liquidation rather than risk-limitation. He acknowledges the soft stop costs him R and sometimes tightens it deliberately. AUDIT CORRECTION - SOFTENED: only 14 of 139 signal posts (10%) publish a candle-close soft SL and only 10 publish the soft+hard pair; 90% of his signals carry a plain numeric stop. Across 217 positions there are 45 stop moves, of which only 15 are a widen, extend, remove or hard-to-manual switch (7% of positions). And all 35 of his losses did close at a stop. The mechanic is real and decisive when it fires, but it is not a standing feature of the book.
  • Cap total risk after DCA at ~1.5R; cap the number of concurrent positions. EXPLICIT but soft. After averaging down he states the aggregate risk in R and gives a ceiling. Separately he repeatedly refuses good-looking setups because too many positions are already open, and closes trades purely to reduce clutter.
  • Lower risk on funded/prop accounts than on live money. EXPLICIT, stated once with specific numbers, and consistent with his early Bybit screenshots being from a CFT funded account.
  • De-risk the capital, not just the price: pull the DCA money back out, take 10% to cover fees, small accounts close fully at TP1. EXPLICIT. Once a DCA fills and the position returns to breakeven he tells members to withdraw the DCA tranche so the trade reverts to original size. Separately he recommends booking ~10% purely to cover fees before moving the stop to entry, so a breakeven stop is not actually a small loss. Guidance is scaled by account size, with small accounts told to take the whole TP rather than run partials.
  • Cut risk after a losing run. BEHAVIOURAL, appears at the end of the sample. After five stops in two days he moved to half risk and then closed a live long at breakeven rather than carry it.

Entry

  • Market entry at CMP with an announced split (50/50, 70/30, 40/40/20). EXPLICIT AND DOMINANT - 240 messages contain 'CMP', and a strict regex finds 139 signal-format posts (Long/Short TICKER + Entry). The template is fixed: Long/Short TICKER, Entry: X CMP, DCA: Y, TP, SL, @Paladin Notify. He states the split in percentages and tells people how to divide the funds. He uses genuine limit orders rarely and flags them ('It's a CMP order, if it's a limit I always write limit').
  • Reserves a DCA tranche below entry - a rescue tool on a minority of trades, not the engine of the win rate. AUDIT CORRECTION - the causal claim is DROPPED. The playbook said the reserved tranche 'is the mechanism that turns a losing entry into a winner'; the outcomes refute it. A DCA tranche is his standard tool for a bad entry, but not a standing feature of every trade: 53 of 139 signal posts (38%) publish a DCA level, 57 of the 200 positions he actually took plan one, and only 30 (14%) ever fill it. Decisively, positions where a DCA filled won 19 and lost 9 (68%), while positions with no DCA fill won 101, lost 26 and scratched 10 (74% including breakevens, 80% excluding) - the DCA cohort performs WORSE, so the reserved tranche cannot be what produces the headline win rate. It does genuinely rescue individual trades ('From almost an SL to a decent TP with a DCA in', msg 959; 'BTC TP hit with a DCA filled so good gains', msg 725), on roughly one trade in seven. The 162-message figure below is a count of DCA chatter, not of signals that reserve a tranche.
  • Two parallel books on BTC: a 0.5R scalp and a 2-3R swing. EXPLICIT — he says so outright and often posts both at once with different SLs and TPs from nearly the same entry, letting followers pick. The scalp carries the win rate, the swing carries the R.
  • Structural long bias — roughly 3 longs published for every short. BEHAVIOURAL AND SELF-ACKNOWLEDGED. AUDIT CORRECTION to the counts: a strict regex finds 139 signal-format posts split 106 long / 33 short (3.2:1); the reconstructed position log has 152 longs and 47 shorts among the 200 positions he actually took (3.2:1). The playbook's '113 longs and 39 shorts of 151' was a soft estimate. The 'roughly 3 longs per short' claim is solid. Longs won 78% of resolved outcomes excluding breakevens, shorts 74% - so the bias is not a handicap in this sample, but his worst stretch (five stops in two days, 19-21 Aug) came from shorting against his own bullish view. He admits 'Idk I'm usually always bullish' and 'I'm the most bullish guy here'.
  • Grades and labels every call before the entry ('risky', 'gamble', 'half risk', 'swing', 'scalp', 'shitcoin'). EXPLICIT AND SYSTEMATIC. Each signal carries a risk label that pre-commits the follower's sizing, and he leans on the label after a loss ('mentioned it was risky so hopefully risk was managed'). 'Gamble trade' is reserved for shitcoins and pre-event entries.
  • Reduce-and-re-add to improve the average and the R. BEHAVIOURAL. When a position is green but the entry was poor, he tells followers to cut size in profit and add the rest lower, explicitly to 'improve R'. He applies the same logic to his own stop placement (tightening the SL to make the ratio better).
  • Trades ideas without official status when he does not want them in the record. BEHAVIOURAL. Ideas posted as 'not an official setup' / 'won't count TP or SL' let him publish calls whose outcomes never touch the monthly win-rate table — including gold, 5m entries, and coins he is not personally taking.

Management

  • Stop to entry / BE after TP1 or ~1R. EXPLICIT RULE HE TEACHES ('Common knowledge but a reminder, SL to Entry after TP1'), instructed in ~44 messages. AUDIT CORRECTION - SOFTENED from 'the follower-facing rule and his own behaviour diverge': he does do it, just selectively - 22 of 217 positions (10%) carry a recorded to-entry stop move - and he makes a point of announcing the exceptions loudly ('will play full setup either SL or TP'). The finding is inconsistency plus loud self-exemption, not outright divergence.
  • He takes one full TP and no partials — while telling followers to take partials. EXPLICIT AND CENTRAL TO HIS IDENTITY: 'Since I don't take partials and take only 1TP so calculating my real R is very easy!' He frames partial-taking as inflating other traders' R. THE PLAYBOOK'S STRONGEST CONTRADICTION, CONFIRMED BY AUDIT AND KEPT AS-IS: on 2026-06-11 at 15:59 he wrote 'I'm still in BTC long from 62.2k I only took 25% at 63k'; at 22:42 the SAME DAY he wrote 'Made 3.2R today, that's realized without any partials, I don't take partials!'. Behaviourally, 43 of 217 positions carry a recorded partial exit - 47 partial exits in total, sized 50% (x11), 25% (x9), 20% (x9), 70% (x3), and one each at 30/40/60/75/10%. The only mitigation is that his July stats line reads '23.5R (Without Partials)', i.e. he claims the ACCOUNTING excludes partials - but that is a different claim from 'I don't take partials', which he states flatly and repeatedly.
  • Discretionary early exit - he closes manually, below his own target, and manual closes never lose. AUDIT REPLACEMENT for the playbook's 'breakeven exits framed as discipline'. Literal breakeven exits are too rare to carry the win rate (only 10-11 of 217 positions end BE), but the mechanism sitting next to them is bigger and cleaner. He closes MANUALLY, on his own read, usually before the published target - and manual closes essentially never lose. Of the 62 positions closed by discretionary exit, 61 are wins, 1 is breakeven, and ZERO are losses. Every one of his 35 losses arrived through a stop. Only 45 of 120 wins (38%) actually reached a target he had published; at least 26 wins were manual closes booked SHORT of the stated TP (BTC 2026-06-17 exited 63,923 against a published 65,000; BB 2026-05-14 exited 0.0371 against a published 0.39; SOL 2026-06-11 exited 67.24 against 68). There are more manual closes (62) than take-profits (45). Breakeven and 'small profits' exits - 44 messages, 15 of them using 'small profits' explicitly - are simply the most extreme version of the same act, framed as discipline. Followers who set the published TP and waited would have had a materially different, and worse, experience than his tally implies.
  • Small, quickly-taken targets: 0.5-0.8R on scalps. EXPLICIT IN HIS OWN WORDS; ONLY HALF-CONFIRMED BY THE RECONSTRUCTION. He states BTC scalps are '90% WR but 0.5R TPs', that his average TP was 0.64R in May, and that his R is '0.5-0.8R on avg' - 31 messages state a figure in that band - and defends it because 'there are so many TPs that 2 trades cover 1SL easily'. AUDIT CORRECTION: of 120 winning positions only 27 carry a stated R, and their median is 1.00R (mean 1.05R); 11 of 27 are <=0.8R, 18 of 27 are <=1.0R, 8 are exactly 0.5R and 2 are >=2R. So the observable win distribution centres on 1R, not 0.5-0.8R, and that sample is self-selected because he reports R when it flatters. The playbook's 'CONFIRMED BY HIS OWN STATS' is downgraded: his own stats confirm it, the record only half-confirms it. Median hold is 17.2 hours (mean 33.9, max 453), consistent with the fast-target claim.
  • Manual take-profit; resting TP orders are removed or overridden. EXPLICIT from the first week ('I take manual TPs but you can set in case'). He often removes a set TP to extend the target, or closes early before the TP because of a rejection. This gives him discretion to book a small win at any moment - and it is the operational half of the discretionary-exit mechanic above.
  • Widening, making manual, or removing the stop rather than taking the loss - rare, but decisive when it happens. BEHAVIOURAL, and directly contradicts his own teaching. He has extended stops mid-trade, switched a hard stop to 'manual 4h close', held past a stop he had published, run an ETH short with no stop at all, and once removed his BTC stop entirely with the reasoning 'if I get stopped I'll short again so not gonna accept my SL here'. AUDIT CORRECTION - SOFTENED: documented 15 times across 217 positions (7%), not habitually. He also states the opposite instinct - 'don't want a trade running publicly without SL' (msg 550) - and 90% of the time he leaves the stop where he put it. ALSO FOLDED IN HERE (moved out of what_he_never_does, where it was refuted): the claim that he never lets a public signal run without a stated stop does not hold. He ran the 1840 ETH short with no stop for at least a day AND publicly invited followers into it - 'I don't have a SL for this, maybe 2k? But I'm using 1% margin with Max Lev if anyone wants to join' (msg 853) - while calling it 'personal'.
  • Re-run the identical setup after it works. BEHAVIOURAL. When a level-based BTC setup pays, he immediately re-posts the same entry/DCA/TP/SL and trades it again, sometimes back-to-back within days, and counts each as a separate win.
  • Explicit percentage instructions to followers at every milestone. EXPLICIT AND CONSTANT. He converts every update into an actionable size instruction — 'take 20-25% here', 'take 10-20% MAX', 'only take 25-40% and save majority', '50% here and remaining 50% at X'. He also caps how much followers should take when he wants them to hold.
  • Add to a position that is already green ('you don't add margin to a green trade unless you're confident'). BEHAVIOURAL AND EXPLICIT. Distinct from DCA-down: when a trade is working and he is confident he increases size, then targets the same level for a bigger result. He also converts a half-risk position to full risk once it is above breakeven.

How to read a card. Left panel is what he published before the trade; right panel is what the messages and screenshots show he actually did. The R strip plots both on one scale where his own stop distance equals 1R, so you can see at a glance whether an exit reached the target he had named. An amber dot next to the result means parts of the record had to be inferred — the trust note at the bottom of the card says which parts.

Blank means he never posted the number; nothing here is calculated or assumed on his behalf. 180 of 200 taken positions carried a published stop, 118 a published target, 57 a published DCA level (only 30 of those ever filled). 43 positions simply stop being mentioned — they are marked never resolved rather than guessed.
